vignette:
At 71, Linh Tran came to treatment still speaking about the period of captivity as something that had never fully ended, even though many years had passed. A divorced Vietnamese American woman who had spent decades building a meticulous career as a financial analyst, she described the traumatic event with the flat precision she brought to spreadsheets, but the details landed with unmistakable force. During the captivity, she had been confined in a place where she could not leave, could not decide when to sleep, and could not count on anyone in authority to step in and stop what was happening. What remained most vivid to her was not a single image so much as the total experience of being trapped under other people’s control, cut off from ordinary protections, and left to endure it while the world outside continued as if nothing were wrong. She had come to believe that the people and institutions that should have protected her had failed in a fundamental way. That conviction did not sound abstract when she said it; it sounded like an old injury she still touched every day.

In the months after she was no longer captive, Linh found that certain feelings arrived with a force that was out of proportion to whatever was happening around her. Fear could come first, but just as often it was anger, shame, guilt, or a sickened sense of horror that washed over her before she could explain it. She tried very hard not to think about the trauma. If a memory edged in, she redirected herself immediately, cleaning a surface, checking numbers, turning on the television, or forcing her mind onto practical tasks. Yet just as often, her thoughts moved in the opposite direction, circling around how life would have been different if the captivity had never happened. She would imagine a version of herself who had moved through the years with more ease, who had not measured every room for safety, who had not come to feel set apart from other people by something foul and ineradicable. Those thoughts left her grieving, but she returned to them repeatedly.

Over time, safety narrowed. Linh could still function, and to outside observers she often appeared composed, but she only felt truly safe in a very limited set of places. Her apartment became one of them because she could control the locks, the lighting, and the arrangement of the rooms. The office where she worked as a financial analyst did not feel safe in the same way, but there were a few zones within it that she could tolerate: her own desk, the break room when it was empty, the hallway closest to the exit. If coworkers suggested after-hours drinks or asked her to stay late in a conference room to go over quarterly figures, she often found reasons to decline. At work she was still highly competent, but she moved through the day with an unspoken map in her head of where she could and could not settle.

Night was consistently worse. As daylight faded, Linh felt her body tighten, as if darkness itself removed the last thin layer of protection. She stayed up very late on purpose, postponing sleep until exhaustion overtook her. She told herself that if she remained awake, alert, and in control, she would not be caught off guard. Even in her apartment, she checked sounds at night more carefully than she did during the day, listening for movement in the hall outside her door, pausing over every shift in the building. By morning she was often tired and brittle. Small frustrations at work—a revised deadline, a software error, a colleague asking for a last-minute change in a report—could leave her feeling overwhelmed and ashamed. She had come to believe she could not deal with even the slightest upset anymore, and each moment of strain seemed to confirm that view.

Another part she disclosed quietly, and only after some hesitation, was a lasting sense of contamination. She did not mean ordinary dirt. She meant that what happened during the captivity seemed to have marked her in a way that washing could not touch. There were days when she changed clothes more than once after coming home, wanting to shed the feeling of being unclean. She was careful about who came into her space and uncomfortable with physical closeness, not because she thought other people would literally contaminate her, but because the old sense of defilement could flare so suddenly.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of a smaller, harder truth: her life had become organized around enduring, restricting, and outwaiting things. Recently, after staying late to finish an analysis, she noticed the office emptying and felt a rush of fear so intense that she had to stop working and sit motionless at her desk until another employee passed by. The incident frightened her less because it was new than because it showed her how small her safe world had become. She came to treatment wanting relief, though she said this cautiously, as if hope itself might be risky. What frightened her most was the possibility that she would spend the rest of her life this way—awake into the night, avoiding her own mind, and never again feeling fully clean or protected anywhere beyond a few carefully defended places.
